concepts.name: The flow matching training loop
concepts.summary: Five lines: sample data x₁, sample noise x₀ ~ N(0,1), sample a time t, build x_t = (1−t)·x₀ + t·x₁, and take ‖(x₁ − x₀) − net(x_t, t)‖². Worked: x₁=5.0, x₀=1.0, t=0.25 gives x_t=2.0 and target 4.0; a network answering 3.7 pays a loss of 0.09. Sorted into three bins, the VAE and text encoder are FROZEN, the interpolation and velocity target are ARITHMETIC with zero parameters, and exactly ONE thing is LEARNED — the velocity field. At image scale nothing changes but the shapes: x₁ is a (32,32,4) latent, the interpolation runs element-wise over all 4,096 elements, and t stays a single scalar shared by all of them.

concepts.name: Non-uniform sampling of t
concepts.summary: The textbook loop draws t ~ U(0,1); production systems do not. π0 uses its own noise-level sampling strategy, and the Lipman flow matching guide confirms that drawing t from a non-uniform distribution — mathematically equivalent to reweighting the loss — performs better at scale. The reason is that different times pose different problems: near t=0 the point is dominated by the noise draw, near t=1 the field is resolving fine detail, so equal effort everywhere is not the best allocation. Implementations that use Beta(1.5, 1.0) are demonstrating the idea, not reproducing any published schedule.

concepts.name: Caching frozen latents
concepts.summary: Because the VAE encoder and text encoder are frozen, they recompute identical outputs every epoch, so pipelines precompute all latents and embeddings once and let training load tensors — removing the two heaviest forward passes from the loop. Two caveats: augmentation breaks it, because a random crop or flip changes the image and therefore the latent, so a cached latent silently disables the augmentation; and the VAE encoder is stochastic, emitting a distribution rather than a point, so caching one sample discards that variation. The usual fix for the second is to cache mean and standard deviation and re-sample each epoch. Text embeddings have neither problem.
